title: Infra GPU Fleet, Capacity, Networking, IaC & CI/CD — Consolidated Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:
This consolidated playbook documents the operational standards and runbooks for Redwood’s GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC module usage, and CI/CD pipelines for infra changes. The goal is to provide a single reference for predictable capacity, safe changes, and rapid mitigation of outages related to GPU infrastructure.

Scope:
- GPU fleet provisioning (on-demand and reserved pools)
- Capacity forecasting and autoscaling policies
- Cloud account structure and VPC/networking patterns for inference clusters
- Terraform modules and recommended patterns for IaC hygiene
- CI/CD pipeline configuration, gating, and release procedures
- Runbooks for common infra incidents (capacity shortage, node failures, driver/kernel upgrades)

Owners & Contacts:
- Primary owner: infra-engineering (pager: infra-oncall)
- GPU Fleet lead: Marco Diaz (marco@redwood.com)
- Networking lead: Lena Chen (lena@redwood.com)
- IaC/CI owner: Ravi Singh (ravi@redwood.com)
- Oncall rota: see /confluence/eng-infra/eng-sre/oncall-rota (linked in team wiki)

Key Principles:
1. Predictability: maintain >= 99.9% availability for reserved GPU pools and < 200ms median provisioning latency for burst lanes (internal SLO).
2. Safety-first changes: all Terraform changes that touch GPU pools, VPCs, or IAM must pass full CI (plan, security scan, reviewed) and a canary apply before global rollout.
3. Observability: every cluster must export node-level and pod-level GPU metrics (utilization, memory, temperature), and alerts are tied to capacity SLOs and error budgets.
4. Repeatability: use standardized Terraform modules and versioned AMIs/container images for inference nodes.

Capacity Planning and GPU Fleet Strategy:
- Target utilization: 60–75% mean observed utilization for reserved pools during business hours (Pacific). This keeps headroom for transient spikes and maintenance.
- Safety buffer: maintain an explicit 20% headroom in reserved capacity.
- Forecast cadence: weekly automated forecast (historical 4-week moving average + trend) produced every Monday; monthly capacity review with product and SRE.
- Scale policies:
  - Autoscaling (burst lane): scale from 0 -> N with warm pools for < 60s cold-start target.
  - Reserved pool scaling: manual/automated scaling with approval flow for > 10% commit change.

Capacity thresholds (quick reference table):
| Tier | Target utilization | Scale-up threshold | Pager threshold | Preferred instance types |
| -----|-------------------:|-------------------:|---------------:|------------------------- |
| Reserved (prod) | 60–75% | 80% 5m sustained | 85% 1m sustained | a100-80gb, h100-80gb |
| Reserved (non-prod) | 30–50% | 65% 5m | 75% 1m | a100-40gb, a10g |
| Burst/ephemeral | N/A (on-demand) | 70% for pooled lanes | - | gpus with fast provisioning (spot fallback) |

Cloud Accounts & Networking Patterns:
- Account layout: separate accounts/projects for:
  1) Platform (shared infra: VPC peering, logging, observability)
  2) Production reserved GPU clusters
  3) Staging/non-prod clusters
  4) Sandbox / experiments
- VPC design:
  - Dedicated VPC per environment with standardized subnet CIDR blocks.
  - Control-plane components (control plane API, observability) live in private subnets with NAT egress.
  - Worker nodes in dedicated subnets with security groups that restrict egress to required registry and telemetry endpoints.
- Network connectivity:
  - Cross-account VPC peering or Transit Gateway for low-latency routing between control-plane and GPU clusters.
  - Service endpoints for cloud registries (e.g., ECR, GCR) and minimal public internet egress.
  - Firewall rules: restrict SSH/RDP to bastion hosts; block public access to inference node management ports.
- IAM & service accounts:
  - Principle of least privilege on node roles.
  - Separate service accounts for provisioning tooling (Terraform CI runner) vs runtime agents.

Terraform / IaC Modules and Patterns:
- Module registry: core infra modules are published to the internal module registry with semantic versioning (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
- Recommended modules:
  - redwood/vpc (vpc + subnets + route tables)
  - redwood/gpu-cluster (autoscaling groups / node pools, instance profiles, GPU drivers)
  - redwood/iam (service accounts and role bindings)
  - redwood/networking (peering, transit gateway attachments, firewall rules)
  - redwood/observability (metric exporters, logging agents, dashboards)
- Module interface (examples):
  - redwood/gpu-cluster variables: cluster_name, instance_type, desired_capacity, max_capacity, node_image_id, gpu_driver_version, labels (map string), taints (list)
  - Output: node_pool_id, autoscaler_policy_id, node_group_arn
- Best practices:
  1) Pin module versions in root module: module "gpu" { source = "internal/redwood/gpu-cluster" version = "v2.3.1" }
  2) Keep small, focused modules; avoid single monolithic repo for all infra.
  3) Use remote state with state locking (S3+DynamoDB or cloud equivalent).
  4) Run `terraform fmt`, `terraform validate`, and `tflint` in CI.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines for Infra:
- Branching model: trunk-based for module and environment repos. Feature branches for changes > single file.
- Pipeline stages (minimum):
  1) Lint & static analysis: terraform fmt/check, tflint, tfsec (security).
  2) Unit/plan: run `terraform init` + `terraform plan` with a dry-run using the target environment state.
  3) Security & policy checks: run policy-as-code (sentinel/open-policy-agent) validating IAM, public access, and encryption.
  4) Manual review: PR requires two approvers (one infra owner, one security reviewer) for changes to GPU clusters, VPCs, or IAM.
  5) Canary apply: apply to a canary environment or single region pool with health checks.
  6) Rollout: progressive apply to remaining regions/pools with pause windows and automated rollback on health degradation.
- CI tooling: GitHub Actions / CircleCI templates with reusable workflow for module publishes and environment applies.
- Secrets: do not store secrets in repo; use KMS/secret manager and short-lived credentials for CI runners.

Runbooks (high-priority scenarios):
1) Capacity shortage (pager):
   - Symptoms: sustained > 85% reserved pool utilization for > 1 minute, requests queued > threshold, request latency & 429 rate increase.
   - Immediate actions:
     1. Acknowledge pager and create incident channel.
     2. Verify autoscaler health and logs: `kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler` or cloud autoscaler logs.
     3. If autoscaler failing: check IAM permissions for scaling actions, check cloud quota limits.
     4. Temporary mitigations:
        - Promote burst lanes: increase ephemeral pool size via API (runbook CLI script).
        - If using scheduled reserved capacity, trigger emergency reserved instance allocation (follow capacity request checklist).
     5. Longer-term: update forecast and submit capacity increase RFC.
2) Node OOM / GPU driver crash:
   - Symptoms: node-level OOM, GPU drivers crash, nodes NotReady, GPU processes terminated.
   - Steps:
     1. Cordons affected nodes: `kubectl cordon <node>`
     2. Collect logs and driver diagnostics: `dmesg`, `nvidia-smi -q`, kubelet logs.
     3. Drain and replace node: `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data` then recycle instance.
     4. If driver version mismatch: check node image & gpu_driver_version variable in terraform; roll back to known-good driver image or coordinate rolling driver upgrade with change window.
3) Control plane or network partition:
   - Symptoms: control-plane cannot reach worker nodes, cluster API flaps, metrics stop reporting.
   - Steps:
     1. Verify VPC routing and peering health.
     2. Check firewall/security group changes in recent Terraform applies.
     3. If misconfiguration identified, use emergency rollback (see CI/CD section) to revert last apply.

Example commands and snippets:
- Terraform plan for prod (CI runner):
```
terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-terraform-prod"
terraform workspace select prod || terraform workspace new prod
terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan
```
- Promote burst pool (example script):
```
# promote-burst.sh
# usage: ./promote-burst.sh --pool-id P123 --count 10
set -e
POOL_ID="$1"
COUNT="$2"
redwoodctl clusters scale --pool $POOL_ID --replicas $COUNT --reason "emergency-promotion"
```

Safety & Change Windows:
- Non-urgent infra changes: prefer nightly windows (02:00–06:00 PT) with 48h notice for cross-team stakeholders.
- Major driver/kernel upgrades: schedule maintenance windows with canary nodes and rollback plan.
- Emergency changes: document in incident channel and follow post-deploy verification checklist.

Audit, Observability, and Metrics:
- Mandatory metrics: node_gpu_utilization, node_gpu_memory_total/used, pod_gpu_request, pod_gpu_usage, node_temperature_celsius.
- Dashboards: per-region per-pool dashboards with 1m/5m/1h aggregates and alerting thresholds.
- Logs: node agent logs, driver crash dumps, autoscaler logs retained for 30 days (extendable per compliance).

Appendix: Useful links & references
